entities.summary:
Les Centristes, officially known as the Democratic Movement (MoDem), emerged in 2007 as a significant political entity in France, headquartered in rue de Grenelle, Paris. Founded by François Bayrou, the party arose during a period marked by increasing polarization in French politics and sought to embody a centrist alternative. This movement was particularly important in the context of French political history, as it aimed to bridge ideological divides, offering a platform that appealed to moderate voters dissatisfied with the extremes of left and right. Les Centristes have played a crucial role in shaping contemporary political discourse in Western Europe, advocating for social liberalism and pro-European Union policies.

The party's formation coincided with the 2007 presidential elections in France, where Bayrou positioned himself as a viable alternative to the major candidates, Nicolas Sarkozy and Ségolène Royal. Despite finishing third in the first round, he garnered 18.57% of the vote, signaling a significant centrist presence in the electoral landscape. Following the elections, Les Centristes participated in various coalitions, notably aligning with Sarkozy's UMP in the National Assembly, which allowed them to influence legislative agendas while maintaining a distinct identity focused on centrism and pragmatic governance.

The legacy of Les Centristes can be observed in their ongoing influence on French politics and their contributions to the broader European centrist movement. They have helped to redefine political alliances in France, demonstrating that a centrist approach can attract considerable public support and legislative power. Moreover, the party has inspired similar movements across Europe, as the political landscape has increasingly seen the fragmentation of traditional parties and the rise of new centrist alternatives.
